summary:
Randall House asked to license the ESV for a study Bible. They reported:
After petitioning to license the ESV translation, Crossway the publisher who owns the rights to the ESV, denied usage. Known to be Reformed in theology, they cited a reluctance to allow an Arminian set of notes accompanying their text.
Yet Crossway had licensed a Catholic Edition of the ESV, even letting Catholic scholars make some changes to the translation.

CrossWire, whose free SWORD project powers many open-source Bible apps, had stopped paying their annual ESV license fee after Crossway seemed willing to host the ESV for SWORD apps themselves, which would make the license unnecessary. Crossway never did, and instead billed $1,400 in back fees and refused to let CrossWire keep distributing it:
Crossway does not wish to have you do this [distribute from CrossWire servers] with our content, as we have our own servers. We also do not want to make your software or the data files ... available on Crossway's site, as we have our own proprietary API, apps, software, and systems.
Crossway later dropped the back fees, but SWORD apps such as AndBible lost the ESV, and then drew bad reviews from users unaware it was out of their hands: “Poor review due to the fact that ESV version is no longer available.”

Pastor Gabriel Hughes paused his daily podcast of LSB readings, 'Hear the Word of the Lord,' after a copyright problem:
really what shut down the Hear the Word of the Lord podcast, at least temporarily, is that I ran into a copyright issue. I did not know that was going to be a thing, but nonetheless, I had to go through the right channels and avenues and try to clear all of that up.
It relaunched in 2025 with the earlier episodes removed and each description now promoting the LSB's publisher.

The Lockman Foundation and their Japanese partners translated the New Japanese Bible together, then disputed who owned it. Lockman claimed it as “work-for-hire” for having funded the project, though their partners put Lockman's funding at only “perhaps 15 percent.” Lockman's lawyers also argued the translation was derived from their English NASB. The partners' field chairman responded:
This, of course, is ridiculous on the face of it, because Lockman exists to promote translations of the Bible from the original languages.
The translators kept the copyright in Japan, reportedly paying Lockman a large settlement in 1996.

Crossway sent a removal notice to churchsw.org, an Australian website offering free downloads of Bible translations including the ESV. The site's owner believed the Holy Spirit is “the original author and copyright holder of all Bibles,” and that translations of Scripture, being fact, can't be copyrighted.

Christian publishers, led by their trade association the ECPA, threatened legal action against an Australian website (churchsw.org) that offered more than 50 Bible translations for free. Its owner believed the Holy Spirit is “the original author and copyright holder of all Bibles,” and that translations of Scripture, being fact, can't be copyrighted. To settle, he had to remove every copyrighted work from all his websites and agree never to share anything owned by any ECPA member without written permission. ECPA's director said:
This case in Australia, along with the cases we faced in England and Nigeria, represents the value of working concertedly as an industry to protect the intellectual property of ECPA members. We appreciate all that Flagler Law Group did to lead this effort on behalf of our Association and the special efforts of Tyndale House, HarperCollins Christian Publishers, and American Bible Society to halt the infringement of many valuable Bible translations.
Tyndale was one of the three publishers party to the settlement, and the site had offered their NLT.

HarperCollins, which owns Zondervan, the NIV's US publisher, was one of the three publishers party to the settlement, and the site had offered the NIV, NIrV and TNIV.

HarperCollins, Thomas Nelson's parent company, was one of the three publishers party to the settlement, and the site had offered the NKJV and NCV.

We appreciate all that Flagler Law Group did to lead this effort on behalf of our Association and the special efforts of Tyndale House, HarperCollins Christian Publishers, and American Bible Society to halt the infringement of many valuable Bible translations.
American Bible Society was one of the three publishers party to the settlement, and the site had offered their Good News Bible and CEV.

Michael Paul Johnson, later editor of the public domain World English Bible, asked Zondervan, the NIV's US publisher, for permission to use the NIV in his Bible software. He wrote:
Zondervan won't grant such permission unless they get a significant royalty (they quoted me $10,000 + $10/copy distributed) and unless I convince them that my Bible search software is "good enough" for them.
He was refused for not guaranteeing $10,000 in sales a year, even though he could pay the fees.

American Bible Society refused to let Rainbow Missions, the nonprofit behind the public domain World English Bible, publish the Good News Bible, CEV and Versión Popular electronically. The requester reported:
They had decided not to grant my request, based on the lack of security of my Internet distribution method. (Horrors! Someone might read the Gospel without paying for it!)
When promised the texts would be encrypted, ABS refused again, saying they would publish their texts electronically themselves, if at all. The requester added:
Frankly, I feel like I've been ripped off, having contributed to the ABS based on their stated purpose of ‘providing the Holy Scriptures to every man, woman, and child in a language and form each can readily understand, and at a price each can easily afford.’ I fail to comprehend how these go together. This action does not match their mission statement very well.

A Christian radio DJ planned an event where 300 people would read the whole Bible aloud in 15 minutes, each reading a different portion. American Bible Society refused permission to use the CEV, so he used the public domain KJV instead.

Gracious Tech asked to include the CSB in Paper Bible, a free app that lets anyone print Scripture. Lifeway, which publishes the CSB, declined:
Unfortunately, we cannot grant this kind of request ... that allows any user to print from the CSB text themselves or with a print-on-demand printer. While we cannot approve this request, we do acknowledge that this is a great service for alternate language texts that are hard to acquire in certain parts of the world, though.

Gracious Tech asked to include the ESV in Paper Bible, a free app that lets anyone print Scripture. Crossway declined:
We reviewed your request and how your platform functions, and unfortunately it is not something we can grant a license for. We have a formal licensing process for allowing trusted bible publishers to print the ESV text. We do not however grant licenses for end-users to print their own editions, regardless of the amount of text they're printing.

Gracious Tech asked to include the NIV in Paper Bible, a free app that lets anyone print Scripture. Biblica denied the request:
Biblica does not allow our licensees and/or their end users to create additional adaptations of any of its texts, especially for uncontrolled onward distribution.
Gracious Tech then offered to turn off all customisation so users could only print the plain NIV text. Biblica denied that too, saying:
to simply offer the user the option to print out a portion of the text (currently available on YV [YouVersion], BG [BibleGateway], and Biblica.com) would not be unique nor innovative, and unfortunately, we would have to deny that as well.
This is despite the fact that none of those websites offer the ability to create booklets or books of Scripture, the service Paper Bible provides.

Gracious Tech asked to include the NRSVue in Paper Bible, a free app that lets anyone print Scripture. The NCC's rights agent first asked for details such as the “Anticipated first print run quantity” and “Anticipated lifetime sales.” When told the app was free, they still asked for money:
The NCC does license the NRSVue for use in gratis applications. The general terms are an annual licensing fee. The terms we can offer are:
Annual Fee: $1,000

CrossWire, whose free SWORD project powers many open-source Bible apps, asked to include the RSV and NRSV. The NCC had them fill out a detailed form about their organisation and products, then replied:
We appreciate your interest in making the RSV/NRSV available as modules for the Sword Project. However, at this time, we do not authorize any open source uses of the RSV/NRSV. God's blessings on your ministry.

The University of Virginia had offered the RSV free on its website for about a decade, including side by side with the KJV for easy comparison. The NCC had it taken down, and the university explained:
We were recently contacted by the National Council of Churches of Christ, who own the copyright for the Revised Standard Version of the Bible in the USA. They have asked us to remove the text from our website, and we have complied with their request.

Shakespeare's Globe in London marked the KJV's 400th anniversary by having actors read the whole Bible aloud on stage from Palm Sunday to Easter. A few days before it began, the director reportedly received a bill from Cambridge University Press, who administer the Crown's rights to the KJV in the UK, for “a substantial royalty fee for the privilege of reading it publicly.”

Gracious Tech asked SIL/Wycliffe for permission to use their Bible translations in Paper Bible, a free app for printing Scripture. They denied the request, having already given other organisations exclusive rights:
In many cases/languages it would conflict with other license agreements we have with other organisations.
They were still willing to look at specific translations:
if there are no conflicting agreements in place, we will consider your request favourably.
But with over 1,000 translations, going case by case wasn't a realistic option. No translations have been licensed for Paper Bible since.

Gracious Tech asked to include the LSB in Paper Bible, a free app that lets anyone print Scripture. The Lockman Foundation said “the publisher needs to grant permission,” but the publisher, 316 Publishing, declined almost eight months later:
due to restrictions in our agreement with the Lockman Foundation, we are unable to grant permission to use the LSB as part of paper.bible at this time.
Gracious Tech asked Tyndale to include the NLT in Paper Bible, a free app that lets anyone print Scripture. Tyndale never responded.

The German Bible Society told Open Scriptures, a non-profit project building an open database of Scripture, to remove the NA27/UBS4 Greek text from their site:
The German Bible Society holds the copyright of both texts. Please remove our texts from your site until 31st March, 2009 at the latest. Otherwise we are forced to take legal steps.
Open Scriptures removed it the next day and asked how they could license the text. The society replied:
Biblical research and translation work costs a lot of money. Therefore, according to the standing rules of our foundation, we have to earn money with our texts to enable further Bible translations worldwide. Please understand that as a matter of principle we don't license the NA27 or the UBS4 Bible text for open source projects.
The society also demanded Open Scriptures remove their copy of MorphGNT, a freely licensed Greek New Testament database, as “again a copyright infringement.” Zack Hubert then shut down his popular free Greek reader zhubert.com, which was built on MorphGNT. The society later added:
the German Bible Society does not license the Greek New Testament for online use as a matter of principle. This does not only apply to your but to any website. However the Greek Bible text is available for free in our Bible portal www.bibelwissenschaft.de.
In other words, it can be read online, but only on the society's own site.

Zondervan, the NIV's US publisher, refused to license the American NIV to Online Bible for the Mac, a free Bible program, while selling their own competing MacBible software. Pastor Tim Bayly, who tried to mediate, recalled:
The correspondence was eye-opening. In my judgment, it was all about money and not a bit about serving the church.
Online Bible had to use the British NIV instead.

A developer asked to include the NIV in instant.bible, a free, open-source app that searches the Bible as you type. Before considering it, Biblica asked him to answer questions including:
Describe what is unique or innovative about your new product(s) proposal?
Is the product(s) already operational with a significant, stable distribution?
Please explain how the project is funded if it is distributed free of charge.
Is the organization behind the product financially sustainable and stable?
After he answered, Biblica said the request would be discussed at their next team meeting and “You will hear from someone shortly.” He never heard back.

A developer asked to include the ESV in instant.bible, a free, open-source app that searches the Bible as you type, where it would only appear as individual verses in search results. Crossway declined:
Unfortunately our Licensing Team did not approve your formal license request as you did not list a formal organization, and we do not license to individuals. If you do set up an LLC in the future, please feel free to contact us as we'd be more open to granting a license for this project.

SIL/Wycliffe told everyone who had licensed the Hawaii Pidgin Bible through the Digital Bible Library to stop using it:
After much consideration, SIL/WBT has agreed to hand over the rights to the Hawaii Pidgin Bible to Hawaii Pidgin Bible Ministries (HPBM), the rightful owners. This means that all contracts WBT has had with DBL Library Card Holders are now null and void. As such, we ask you to please remove this text from your apps.
The handover was presumably prompted by Hawaii Pidgin Bible Ministries claiming the rights as their own, and anyone who wanted to keep using the text had to start over with a new request to them. Even if SIL/Wycliffe weren't to blame, it shows the risk of licensing Scripture at all: one dispute over ownership was enough to pull a Bible from everywhere it had been shared, the opposite of these organisations' mission to spread God's word.

A college student building a free Scripture memorization web app asked Crossway how he could use the ESV, and why his application for their free API had been rejected. Crossway then approved the API, which limits how much text can be requested and doesn't allow storing it, but said anything beyond that needed a paid license, which they only grant to organisations:
We offer a formal ministry license to organizations which offers the full ESV XML files to store on a noncommercial website/app, and is free of the API restrictions. This comes with an annual fee of $100-250 depending on how the text is distributed, per platform. ... We only license to formal organizations or ministries rather than to individuals ... Crossway is selective in which platforms we license the ESV for, so we ask that you include detailed information and unique features that set your platform apart from existing bible platforms.

Someone asked Crossway to explain two rules on their permissions page:
The ESV may not be translated in whole or in part into any other language.
The ESV text may not be quoted in any publication made available to the public by a Creative Commons license.
The requester asked on behalf of ESV readers doing missionary work in other countries, and developers of open-source Bible software who couldn't use the ESV. Crossway never replied, even after the questions were sent again.

A Bible software developer found that their copy of the LEB was missing text in Genesis 6:4. They asked Logos, which promotes the LEB as “one of the most generously licensed modern English Bibles,” for an up-to-date source file. After two weeks of support staff misunderstanding the request, Logos replied:
We no longer distribute the LEB in standalone file formats like USFM, OSIS, or the custom XML you referred to. The team members involved in the initial distribution of those files are no longer with the company, and the infrastructure for sharing those specific file types is not something we currently maintain for public distribution.
There are currently no official ways to access the LEB text aside from Logos' proprietary software.

A developer applied to use Crossway's free ESV API in an app showing the passages for upcoming Sunday sermons. Crossway declined:
Our Licensing team is not currently approving the pairing of the ESV text with AI-generated text.
He explained that he had only used AI to help write the app's code, and that it simply displayed the ESV text with no AI-generated content, then asked Crossway to reconsider. Crossway never replied, even after a polite follow-up several days later.

Rhythm and Bible, a YouTube channel setting books of the Bible to AI-generated music, with lyrics that are the Scripture text word for word, asked Crossway for permission to use the ESV before releasing their songs on streaming platforms. The channel posted:
Before we go live on streaming platforms we've hit a wall regarding the ESV and copyright. We've applied for permission and we're trusting that comes through
Crossway refused and told them to stop. When the channel asked what this meant for the songs already published, Crossway had those taken down too, as the channel later posted:
We've been advised to remove every video featuring ESV

Gracious Tech noticed that only the first edition of the NET was available in a format easily integrated into software. They asked the owners for the latest edition, to distribute non-commercially within the NET's existing terms. Permission was granted and the required format was provided, but when asked whether those files could be made available for other developers to use, the permissions director suggested:
I want to add something in the text that we can find if the text you distribute makes it into a commercial venture. Put your thinking cap on on [sic] what we may do.. Maybe we repeat a word in a verse in Eccleslastes [sic] or we misspell a word in John
The idea was never acted on, but the file contained unrelated formatting errors, and the latest edition of the NET is still not available in a format that can be easily integrated into software.

An app developer asked the Vietnamese Bible Society for permission to use their Vietnamese translation in their free Bible apps. They declined:
As we do not currently have a policy for providing the text to software applications, we are not able to help you yet. Perhaps from June next year we may be able to discuss this matter with you, so we will plan to get back in touch with you at that time. [translation]
This is despite the translation already being available in some other apps like YouVersion. They never got back to the developer.

After a user requested the Hakha Chin Bible for use in Paper Bible, Gracious Tech asked the Bible Society of Myanmar to license it under CC BY 4.0 so it could legally be included in the app. They never responded.

A Christian who had memorized the ESV New Testament asked Crossway for permission to post free videos of himself reciting it, one chapter each weekday, to inspire others to memorize Scripture. He offered to pay any license fee himself, but Crossway declined:
we have strict audio licensing guidelines that prohibit us from granting permissions for recordings where the ESV would make up 50% or more of the content. Part of the reasoning behind this is that we make the ESV audio freely available on many different platforms, and we prefer to ensure any new audio recordings are done at a high quality by reputable audio publishers.
He replied that he would hire a professional videographer, and even offered to make it a Crossway product for their own channels. Crossway said they were “unable to partner with you on this project,” and would only reconsider if he added enough other material to bring the ESV below half of each video. He worried the extra material would become “filler”:
just content that is added for the purpose of padding the length of something to hit a specific requirement.
Unable to meet Crossway's conditions without compromising the project, he abandoned the idea of reciting the ESV.

A Christian memorizing the ESV New Testament asked Crossway whether he could recite whole books, such as Philippians, from memory at churches. Crossway said reciting live was fine, but that recording it needed permission, “as we see this as a creation of an audio product.” Even a church's own livestream couldn't stay up for long:
We typically would ask that these recordings not be available in perpetuity, but again we would be open to considering them case by case. Usually there is no fee as we would not allow the audio/ video to be available in perpetuity, rather we would allow the church's livestream to be available for about a week then taken down if the recitation of the ESV makes up the majority of the content of the video.
